gm.road_lines: White Outside - White Inside / White Outside - Yellow Inside

items.html: Bolivia has short, white licence plates with blue text. The blue text can be hard to see through the blur, so plates might appear as plain white.

Bolivia only has Generation 3 camera coverage. All of the country was covered by a solid white Google car with no antenna.

NOTE: In Latin America, white cars with no antenna can also be found in Peru and Chile.

Many buildings in Bolivia consist of large red bricks. Buildings often have an ‘unfinished' look.

NOTE: This style of architecture is also common in parts of Peru.

Middle road lines can be all-yellow, yellow and white, or all-white, while outer road lines are always white.

NOTE: Road lines in Chile are always all-white or all-yellow, never a combination of the two. In Peru, you can find roads having outer lines with no middle line. Such outer line-only roads are very rare in Bolivia.
Bolivia has a lot of standard asphalt roads, but concrete slab roads are also fairly common.
There are also a lot of cobblestone roads. These roads often have a specific pattern, with several neat lines of stones separating the more disorganised cobblestones in between.

Bolivia typically uses bulky, white square signposts.

NOTE: Peru typically uses black and white striped “zebra” signposts.

Guardrails sometimes feature yellow and black markings. These markings always have the yellow stripes on the outside.

NOTE: Peru has similar markings. However, in Peru, the markings have the inverse colour scheme: the black stripes are always on the outside.

Two types of utility poles are common in Bolivia:

  • Round concrete poles, often with small pinholes near the top.
  • Wooden poles.

Poles in Bolivia are very inconsistent and should not be relied on too much. Poles can have a variety of pole tops. On rare occasions, you can find Argentina-style concrete poles.

Many wooden utility poles, particularly in the eastern parts of Bolivia’s Street View coverage, are noticeably curvy and look like they are made from locally sourced tree trunks.

NOTE: While you may see slightly bent poles in other places, extremely curvy poles are a very good clue for Bolivia.

Kilometre markers are black and white. The top part is black and features the abbreviation ‘Km’, while the bottom part is white and shows the distance. These markers do not have road numbers.

NOTE: They can look somewhat similar to Argentinian road markers, especially from a distance. The main difference is that the markers in Argentina feature a road number.

Many Bolivians wear traditional clothing, especially women. Folk dress for women typically consists of bowler hats, colourful shawls, and big pleated skirts (pollera).

NOTE: Similar folk dress can sometimes be found in parts of Peru, especially those close to Bolivia.

At the time Bolivia was covered by Street View, its ruling political party was the Movimiento al Socialismo (MAS). Political graffiti often features the words MAS and Evo, short for then-president Evo Morales.

Additionally, many random objects are painted in the party’s colours: black, white, and a large blue field. This distinctive colour scheme is a good clue for Bolivia.
Bolivia has a second official flag, called the Wiphala. It is a square patchwork of seven diagonally arranged colours. It is sometimes seen on government buildings and project signs.

In urban areas, you will often see ads for the telecom company Tigo, with its distinct blue logo. Crucially, this company does not operate in Peru, meaning it can help you solve urban 50-50s.

NOTE: This company does operate in several other Latin American countries, so only use this tip to differentiate between Peru and Bolivia.

If all else fails, and you have a tough 50-50, it can help to look at the colour of the rocks and soil, which often have a distinct reddish tint in Bolivia, more so than the other Andean countries.

This information should be used with a fair amount of caution, as there are many variables. Only use it when you have no other clues available.

Coverage in Bolivia is very limited, both in geographic scope and the density of roads covered.

Only the central and central-western parts of the country have coverage. Most coverage is found in and around the six main cities of La Paz or El Alto, Cochabamba, Oruro, Sucre, Potosi, and Santa Cruz.

These aforementioned six cities have in-depth side-street coverage. Outside these cities, coverage is mostly limited to main roads. Beware that “main road” is a relative concept in Bolivia: many of these, even some that are marked yellow on the map, have large unpaved sections.

The Altiplano (“high plain”) is an immense highland plateau that dominates most of western Bolivia. It is covered in grasslands that range from green to arid. Some parts are suitable for agriculture, whereas other parts are extremely dry. Grass growing in tufts is common (sometimes referred to as “Bolivian hedgehogs” in the community).

NOTE: While it is generally fairly flat, you will often see hills and mountains around you. However, as a general rule, the road itself will be mostly flat.

The grasslands of the Altiplano tend to look more lush in the more northern half: the area close to El Alto and La Paz.

NOTE: Due to seasonal coverage, there are some exceptions to this, but in general this is a good rule of thumb to distinguish between the different parts of the Altiplano.

Conversely, the Altiplano looks more arid in the more southern half: around Oruro, and the roads going southwest towards Chile.

NOTE: There is one major exception to this: one driving side of the divided part of Ruta 1 looks somewhat green all the way up to Oruro (due to this coverage being captured in a different season).

Lake Titicaca, on the border with Peru, is the most significant body of water in Bolivia. It is located entirely within the Altiplano. It can be seen from two roads:

  • The section of Ruta 1 between Desaguadero and Guaqui. Here, the lake will always be to your north.
  • The section of Ruta 2 between San Pablo de Tiquina and Batallas. Here, the lake will mostly be to your south or west.

The landscape around Titicaca is very green, compared to most of the western half of Bolivia.

If you are surrounded by tall mountains, you are likely in the Andes, which goes roughly northwest to southeast in between the Altiplano and the Amazon rainforest.

NOTE: The Altiplano has several smaller and solitary mountains.

The area east of the Andes is very green and tropical, with lots of agriculture – especially around Santa Cruz. This area is mostly very flat, though you will see large hills on some of the roads closer to the Andes. The soil tends to have a pink colour.
Within this tropical area, coverage on unpaved roads is only found around Santa Cruz. These roads again prominently have the pink soil that is very characteristic of the area east of Andes.
Aside from being a useful identifier for the country, cobblestone roads are mainly found in and southeast of Cochabamba. They also appear around Sucre and, very rarely, in La Paz.
Only a couple of cities and towns in Bolivia have a lot of sidestreet coverage. Most of the cities can be easily and consistently distinguished from each other using a few basic tips.

La Paz and El Alto are twin cities that together form one big metropolitan area. However, despite being located right next to each other, they each have a very different look. See the tips below for more information.

La Paz is a very hilly city. Most of La Paz itself is situated in meandering valleys, surrounded by hills that often tend to be covered in green vegetation (as opposed to the more dry hillsides found in many other Bolivian urban areas).
Downtown La Paz is the only place in Bolivia where you will find very tall buildings (10+ storeys).

In many parts of La Paz, you can see these heavily eroded, pillar-like rock formations on the hillsides. They consist of a very recognizable yellow-beige sandstone.

Of the big cities with coverage in Bolivia, these rock formations are essentially unique to La Paz.

El Alto is situated on a very flat, highland plateau. It looks much drier and dustier than La Paz. The layout of its streets is also more regular and grid-like.

The city appears like an unending mess of semi-finished red brick buildings, even more so than other cities in Bolivia. Some neighbourhoods have a very rundown, desolate look.
This type of pavement, consisting of rectangular grey bricks with slightly wavy edges, is very common in El Alto.

In El Alto, you can sometimes see a local type of architecture referred to as Neo-Andean. Buildings in this style are colourful, with elaborate, futuristic-looking façades. The style is really unique and is almost completely limited to El Alto.
Gates and doors in El Alto are sometimes painted with a gradient pattern, usually dark green to light green, or red to yellow.

Cochabamba is situated in a large flat valley, where you will almost always see an imposing wall of mountains to your north. This is the single most useful and consistent way of distinguishing this city from other places in Bolivia.

Of all the major cities in Bolivia, Oruro is situated in by far the most dry landscape.

In Oruro, you will also usually be able to see a large dry hill to your west, in an otherwise mostly flat and very arid landscape.

NOTE: Potosí is also located in an arid landscape. However, it is considerably hillier.
Sucre is situated in a very hilly landscape, and as a result you can see many elevation changes in its streets. Uniquely, you can see these round, tree-covered hills in many parts of the city.

Sucre has a well-preserved historic city centre, with lots of old colonial buildings. The downtown area can be recognized by the white walls, orange tiled roofs, and generally more historic look than other places in Bolivia.
Potosí is also situated in a very hilly landscape, like Sucre. However, its landscape is much more arid, with little to no trees atop the hills.

In many parts of Potosí, you can see this colossal pyramid-shaped mountain called Cerro Rico. It is famous for having massive quantities of silver ore, and as a result its surface is stripped bare by extensive mining – which is distinctly visible in the street view coverage.

Santa Cruz is the only large Bolivian city located in a tropical (and flat) landscape.

Note that there are several smaller towns around Santa Cruz that look essentially identical. Some of these have extensive side-road coverage too.

Ruta 1 west of El Alto is a paved road that runs through green grasslands. The road itself is mostly flat, but you will usually see hills nearby. On the road, you will often see numbers marked in white paint.

Near the western end of the road, close to Desaguadero and the border with Peru, you will be able to see Lake Titicaca to your north.

NOTE: This road can look very similar to Ruta 2 northwest of El Alto. Road angles can help if you are not sure.

The section of Ruta 3 around Pongo, northeast of La Paz, can easily be recognised by the breathtaking views of enormous mountains, which are often surrounded by low-hanging clouds. The mountains are also recognizable by their dark grey rocks lightly covered in greenish grass.

The N Yungas Road (also popularly known as Death Road), is a bendy, small and unpaved road, high up in the mountains east of La Paz. The vegetation is very tropical. The coverage in the southern part of the road is very foggy. True to its unofficial name, this road looks like a very dangerous drive. You can sometimes see some daring cyclists.

NOTE: The northern half of this road looks less foggy and dangerous. However, it should still be recognizable, as it is the only dirt road meandering through jungle hills in Bolivia.

Ruta 1 and 4 between La Paz and Oruro is a large divided highway that runs through the Altiplano landscape of western Bolivia.

It is the only large, divided highway in the entire country. There are smaller, divided roads in and near some urban areas, but those should be easily distinguishable based on landscape and road size.

A long section of Ruta 4 has a distinctive square smudge on the front left of the camera. This coverage starts in the altiplano near Vila Vila, going east through Cochabamba, all the way to Buena Vista in the flat Amazonian part of Bolivia.

Around Morochata, northwest of Cochabamba on Ruta 25, there is a small isolated piece of coverage that looks extremely similar to Peru. It is a dirt road that meanders through a mountainous landscape. Knowing this road can be extremely helpful for country streak purposes.

The western part of this road is located in a green mountain landscape, with fields on the mountain slopes and lots of eucalyptus trees around.

Towards the east, it transitions into a more arid high altitude landscape that still looks very similar to Peru.

Ruta 1 between Machacamarca and Guindal runs through an arid landscape where you will often see patches of snow on the hilltops, and sometimes even next to the road. Weather conditions range from cloudy to fully overcast, lending this coverage a gloomy look.

The aforementioned road can be regionguessed even more precisely. See the next two tips.

The section north of Challapata runs in a general NNW direction, with straight roads in flat terrain, with hills on one or both sides. Weather conditions are a little bit better, with some of the sky visible, especially when looking south.
The section southeast of Challapata tends to be more curvy and hilly. The weather is much worse, with grey skies.

The section of Ruta 7 between Mairana and the outskirts of Santa Cruz has coverage with a camera bug that causes a visual glitch. It is a distinctive, neon-like discoloration, that (depending on the road angle) is usually more or less to your north.

NOTE: This glitch can also rarely be found in some limited areas in and around Santa Cruz. In these areas, the glitch is often not as severe.

The roads around the town of Mataral have recognizable coverage: a very green, hilly landscape, and sunny weather with only a couple of clouds. While the hills are very green, the vegetation is not very dense, and quite low.

This coverage is limited to Ruta 7 from Comarapa to Mairana, and Ruta 22 to Vallegrande. Other roads in Bolivia with similar vegetation tend to either have different weather (overcast) or terrain (more flat).
In the aforementioned Mataral area, you will often see large cacti hiding between the bushes, as well as trees with yellow flowers.

The eastern section of Ruta 4, east of Santa Cruz, runs in a general east-west direction, through a mostly flat, green landscape. In some places, you can see some low hills. This road has both asphalt and concrete pad sections.
The section of Ruta 5 around Chaco, just north of Sucre, has distinct sunset coverage. Most of this road has concrete pavement, and meanders through semi-arid hills.
The section of Ruta 4, southwest of Patacamaya, runs through a semi-arid grassland landscape. Many parts of that road between Patacamaya and Callapa have worn-down grainy asphalt.

On the southwesternmost section of Ruta 4, you can usually see the Nevado Sajama, an isolated snow-capped volcano that is very distinct and unlike any other mountain in Bolivia.

When you see Sajama, you will always be south of Callapa and the Desaguadero River. However, you will not always be able to see it on this section of the road, as it is often hidden by hills.

NOTE: The only other place where you can see Nevado Sajama is coverage in the National Park, which is recognizable by its unique Google car.
The section of Ruta 6 between Tarabuco and Zudáñez is paved with extremely light-coloured concrete, bordering on white. This pavement is very recognizable and unique to this road.

Between the villages of Villa Vitalina and Coipasa, there is an isolated stretch of coverage where the Google car drove through extremely arid desert terrain. This small road is located close to the southwestern end of Ruta 12, near the Chilean border. It can be hard to spot on the map, because it blends in with the salt flat.

Closer to Villa Vitalina, the car drove over the salt flat. Closer to Coipasa, the car drove on an unpaved dirt road, where you can see cone-shaped volcanic hills. In both parts, there is virtually no vegetation.

Sajama National Park was covered by this unique Google car: it has a black roof rack with a series of metal bars.

The coverage is on an unpaved road surrounded by fluffy bushes. The Nevado Sajama volcano is always visible. The car briefly drove through the small village of Tomarapi, which can be recognized by its traditional buildings with adobe walls and thatched roofs.

steps.title: Maps and resources
steps.html:
GeoGuessr’s own official maps are not very good, for a variety of reasons. Plonk It recommends the following maps instead:

  • An Arbitrary Bolivia (map link) - 25k+ locs with a slight focus on smaller rural roads.
  • A Balanced Bolivia (map link) - 40k+ locs balanced by department.
  • Bolivian Pain (map link) - The final boss for all the Bolivia Nerds out there. Includes almost no towns or main roads.

In addition, here are some resources to help you practise Bolivia:

  • Plonk It Bolivia (map link) - This map contains locations for practising each meta in the Plonk It Bolivia guide from step 2 to 3.

lm.name: Chile Border Desert
lm.note: Between the villages of Villa Catalina and Coipasa, there is an isolated stretch of coverage where the Google car drove through extremely arid desert terrain. In both parts, there is virtually no vegetation.

lm.name: Lake Titicaca
lm.note: Lake Titicaca, on the border with Peru, is the most significant body of water in Bolivia. It is located entirely within the Altiplano. The landscape around Titicaca is very green, compared to most of the western half of Bolivia.

lm.name: Northern Altiplano
lm.note:
The grasslands of the Altiplano tend to look more lush in the more northern half: the area close to El Alto and La Paz.

NOTE: Due to seasonal coverage, there are some exceptions to this, but in general this is a good rule of thumb to distinguish between the different parts of the Altiplano.

lm.name: Sajama National Park
lm.note: Sajama National Park was covered by this unique Google car: it has a black roof rack with a series of metal bars. The coverage is on an unpaved road surrounded by fluffy bushes. The Nevado Sajama volcano is always visible. The car briefly drove through the small village of Tomarapi, which can be recognized by its traditional buildings with adobe walls and thatched roofs.

lm.name: Santa Cruz Area
lm.note: Within the tropical area of Bolivia, coverage on unpaved roads is only found around Santa Cruz. These roads again prominently have the pink soil that is very characteristic of the area east of Andes.

lm.name: Southern Altiplano
lm.note:
The Altiplano looks more arid in the more southern half: around Oruro, and the roads going southwest towards Chile.

NOTE: There is one major exception to this: one driving side of the divided part of Ruta 1 looks somewhat green all the way up to Oruro (due to this coverage being captured in a different season).

lm.name: Wider Santa Cruz Area
lm.note: The area east of the Andes is very green and tropical, with lots of agriculture – especially around Santa Cruz. This area is mostly very flat, though you will see large hills on some of the roads closer to the Andes. The soil tends to have a pink colour.

lm.name: Unfinished Look
lm.note:
• Many buildings in Bolivia consist of large red bricks.
  • Buildings often have an ‘unfinished' look.

--- NOTE:

  • This style of architecture is also common in parts of Peru.

lm.name: Unique Guardrail
lm.note:
Guardrails sometimes feature yellow and black markings. These markings always have the yellow stripes on the outside.

NOTE: Peru has similar markings. However, in Peru, the markings have the inverse colour scheme: the black stripes are always on the outside.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner
lm.name: Curvy poles
lm.note: Many wooden utility poles, particularly in the eastern parts of Bolivia are noticeably curvy and appear to be made from locally sourced tree trunks.

lm.name: Death road
lm.note: Northeast of La Paz, there is an unpaved road that is cloudy and wet and narrow and looks like a nightmare to drive. Yet, apparently, it is frequented by mountain bikers a whole lot.

lm.name: City Roads, Cochabamba
lm.note: Cochabamba is situated in a large flat valley, where you will almost always see an imposing wall of mountains to your north. This is the single most useful and consistent way of distinguishing this city from other places in Bolivia.

lm.name: City Roads, Eastern La Paz
lm.note:
La Paz and El Alto are twin cities that together form one big metropolitan area. However, despite being located right next to each other, they each have a very different look.

In many parts of La Paz but primarily in the urban East and surrounding roads, you can see these heavily eroded, pillar-like rock formations on the hillsides. They consist of a very recognizable yellow-beige sandstone (see image). Landslides seem to be common.

Of the big cities with coverage in Bolivia, these rock formations are essentially unique to La Paz.

The further out you go from the city, the more it turns to rolling green hills and patchy high altitude farmland.

Further East still and you begin to see the snow capped peaks of Layqa Qullu and Illimani.

lm.name: City Roads, El Alto
lm.note:
El Alto is situated on a very flat, highland plateau. It looks much drier and dustier than La Paz. The layout of its streets is also more regular and grid-like.

The city appears like an unending mess of semi-finished red brick buildings, even more so than other cities in Bolivia. Some neighbourhoods have a very rundown, desolate look.

Pavement consisting of rectangular grey bricks with slightly wavy edges is very common in El Alto (see image).

You can sometimes see a local type of architecture referred to as Neo-Andean. Buildings in this style are colourful, with elaborate, futuristic-looking façades. The style is really unique and is almost completely limited to El Alto (see image).

Gates and doors are sometimes painted with a gradient pattern, usually dark green to light green, or red to yellow (see image).

lm.name: City Roads, La Paz Central
lm.note:
La Paz and El Alto are twin cities that together form one big metropolitan area. However, despite being located right next to each other, they each have a very different look.

La Paz is a very hilly city. Most of La Paz itself is situated in meandering valleys, surrounded by hills that often tend to be covered in green vegetation as opposed to the more dry hillsides found in many other Bolivian urban areas (see image).

Downtown La Paz is the only place in Bolivia where you will find very tall buildings of 10+ storeys (see image).

lm.name: City Roads, Oruro
lm.note:
Of all the major cities in Bolivia, Oruro is situated in by far the most dry landscape.

In Oruro, you will also usually be able to see a large dry hill to your west, in an otherwise mostly flat and very arid landscape.

NOTE: Potosí is also located in an arid landscape. However, it is considerably hillier.

lm.name: City Roads, Potosi
lm.note:
Potosí is also situated in a very hilly landscape, like Sucre. However, its landscape is much more arid, with little to no trees atop the hills.

In many parts of Potosí, to the South you can see this colossal pyramid-shaped mountain called Cerro Rico. It is famous for having massive quantities of silver ore, and as a result its surface is stripped bare by extensive mining – which is distinctly visible in the street view coverage (see image).

lm.name: City Roads, Santa Cruz & Suburbs
lm.note:
Santa Cruz is the only large Bolivian city located in a tropical (and flat) landscape.

Note that there are several smaller towns around Santa Cruz that look essentially identical. Some of these have extensive side-road coverage too.

lm.name: City Roads, Sucre
lm.note:
Sucre is situated in a very hilly landscape, and as a result you can see many elevation changes in its streets. Uniquely, you can see these round, tree-covered hills in many parts of the city.

It has a well-preserved historic city centre, with lots of old colonial buildings. The downtown area can be recognized by the white walls, orange tiled roofs, and generally more historic look than other places in Bolivia.

lm.name: Cobbled Road, From Sillani
lm.note:
Though fairly common in cities (especially Cochabamba), there are only a handful of rural cobbled roads, and they can be differentiated with some practice. Five exist to the East of Cochabamba, and three to the East of Sucre. Ruta 23 is the only main road with coverage of a cobbled section.

South East of Sucre, the most eastern of the three starts at Sillani and heads roughly South from there.

The sun is always visible to the NNW, and you will often see a drainage canal running alongside the road.

lm.name: Cobbled Road, North of Sacaba
lm.note:
Though fairly common in cities (especially Cochabamba), there are only a handful of rural cobbled roads, and they can be differentiated with some practice. Five exist to the East of Cochabamba, and three to the East of Sucre. Ruta 23 is the only main road with coverage of a cobbled section.

North of Sacaba to the North East of Cochabamba lies a short unnamed section of cobbled road winding through the mountains with the city visible south.

The sun is always visible to the NW.

If you see Eucalyptus on a cobbled road, you are likely in the sections around Cochabamba rather than those around Sucre.

lm.name: Cobbled Road, Ruta 23, Section SE of Cochabamba
lm.note:
Though fairly common in cities (especially Cochabamba), there are only a handful of rural cobbled roads, and they can be differentiated with some practice. Five exist to the East of Cochabamba, and three to the East of Sucre. Ruta 23 is the only main road with coverage of a cobbled section.

South East of Cochabamba lies a cobbled section of Ruta 23, heading in a NW/SE direction through grassy hills.

The Western part features clear skies with the sun in the NE and patchy tree coverage.

The Eastern part is mainly overcast, and has more vegitation, thickening out to forested hills as you travel East.

If you see Eucalyptus on a cobbled road, you are likely in the sections around Cochabamba rather than those around Sucre.

lm.name: Cobbled Road, Tarabuco To ICLA
lm.note:
Though fairly common in cities (especially Cochabamba), there are only a handful of rural cobbled roads, and they can be differentiated with some practice. Five exist to the East of Cochabamba, and three to the East of Sucre. Ruta 23 is the only main road with coverage of a cobbled section.

South East of Sucre, the most Western of the three starts at Tarabuco and heads predominantly South East to ICLA.

The sun is always visible between N and NNE, and you will usually see a drainage canal running alongside the road.\

lm.name: Cobbled Road, Through Cliza
lm.note:
Though fairly common in cities (especially Cochabamba), there are only a handful of rural cobbled roads, and they can be differentiated with some practice. Five exist to the East of Cochabamba, and three to the East of Sucre. Ruta 23 is the only main road with coverage of a cobbled section.

South East of Cochabamba lies a short section of cobbled road passing through Cliza in a NW/SE direction.

In the Western stretch, some of the cobble is partially paved over with bits showing through, and sometimes Cochabamba's north imposing wall of mountains is visible.

The Eastern stretch features a low sun angle.

The sun direction ranges from N to NW.

If you see Eucalyptus on a cobbled road, you are likely in the sections around Cochabamba rather than those around Sucre.

lm.name: Cobbled Road, Through Tarabuquillo
lm.note:
Though fairly common in cities (especially Cochabamba), there are only a handful of rural cobbled roads, and they can be differentiated with some practice. Five exist to the East of Cochabamba, and three to the East of Sucre. Ruta 23 is the only main road with coverage of a cobbled section.

South East of Sucre, the middle the three snakes roughly N/S passing through Tarabuquillo.

The sun is always visible to the NW, and you will sometimes see a drainage canal running alongside the road.\

lm.name: Cobbled Road, Through Tin Tin
lm.note:
Though fairly common in cities (especially Cochabamba), there are only a handful of rural cobbled roads, and they can be differentiated with some practice. Five exist to the East of Cochabamba, and three to the East of Sucre. Ruta 23 is the only main road with coverage of a cobbled section.

South East of Cochabamba lies a short section of cobbled road passing through Tin Tin in a NE/SW direction.

You should be able to make out a dark smudge glitch when facing forward, and you will often be able to see a small stream to the West of the road.

The sun is always visible to the NW, and this section has some sunset coverage.

If you see Eucalyptus on a cobbled road, you are likely in the sections around Cochabamba rather than those around Sucre.

lm.name: Cobbled Road, Totora To Aiquile
lm.note:
Though fairly common in cities (especially Cochabamba), there are only a handful of rural cobbled roads, and they can be differentiated with some practice. Five exist to the East of Cochabamba, and three to the East of Sucre. Ruta 23 is the only main road with coverage of a cobbled section.

South East of Cochabamba, lies a long section of cobbled road snaking through mountains from Totora To Aiquile in a N/S direction. This is the furthest East of the Cochabamba adjacent cobbled roads.

There is sometimes a blur glitch visible when facing forward.

The sun is always visible between N and NNW.

The Southern part of this road in particular features large cacti including Cereus Stenogonus and Harrisia Trtracantha.

If you see Eucalyptus on a cobbled road, you are likely in the sections around Cochabamba rather than those around Sucre.

lm.name: La Paz To Huayna Potosi Mountain
lm.note:
This rocky mountain road heads North out of La Paz up towards the Huayna Potosi Mountain through grassy rolling hills.

The city is visible South in the lower section, and the mountain visible North in the upper section.

A river & several lakes are visible to the West of the road in many locations, as well as irrigation channels, often with running water.

The sky is mostly overcast.

lm.name: N Yungas Road (AKA Death Road)
lm.note:
The N Yungas Road (also popularly known as Death Road), is a small, bendy and unpaved road, high up in the mountains east of La Paz with very tropical vegetation.

The coverage in the southern part of the road is very foggy. True to its unofficial name, this road looks like a very dangerous drive.

You can sometimes see some daring cyclists.

NOTE: The northern half of this road looks less foggy and dangerous. However, it should still be recognizable, as it is the only dirt road meandering through jungle hills in Bolivia.

lm.name: Roads near Death Road
lm.note:
Paved roads which vibe like a combination of the Pongo section and Death Road but higher in the mountains.

Clouds and fog, sometimes fogging up the camera.

lm.name: Ruta 1 & 4, La Paz to Oruro
lm.note:
Ruta 1 and 4 between La Paz and Oruro is a large divided highway that runs through the Altiplano landscape of western Bolivia.

It is the only large, divided highway in the entire country. There are smaller, divided roads in and near some urban areas, but those should be easily distinguishable based on landscape and road size.

lm.name: Ruta 1, Challapata To Guindal
lm.note:
Ruta 1 between Machacamarca and Guindal runs through an arid landscape where you will often see patches of snow on the hilltops, and sometimes even next to the road. Weather conditions range from cloudy to fully overcast, lending this coverage a gloomy look.

This section southeast of Challapata tends to be more curvy and hilly. The weather is much worse, with grey skies.

lm.name: Ruta 1, Machacamarca To Challapata
lm.note:
Ruta 1 between Machacamarca and Guindal runs through an arid landscape where you will often see patches of snow on the hilltops, and sometimes even next to the road. Weather conditions range from cloudy to fully overcast, lending this coverage a gloomy look.

This section north of Challapata runs in a general NNW direction, with straight roads in flat terrain, with hills on one or both sides. Weather conditions are a little bit better, with some of the sky visible, especially when looking south.

lm.name: Ruta 1, West of El Alto
lm.note:
Ruta 1 west of El Alto is a paved road that runs through green grasslands. The road itself is mostly flat, but you will usually see hills nearby. On the road, you will often see numbers marked in white paint.

Near the western end of the road, close to Desaguadero and the border with Peru, you will be able to see Lake Titicaca to your North.

NOTE: This road can look very similar to Ruta 2 northwest of El Alto. Road angles can help if you are not sure.

lm.name: Ruta 12 & Unnamed Roads Around Corque
lm.note: Around Corque, this section of Ruta 12, and the unnamed road branching off it heading South, are predominantly paved tarmac (as opposed to cracked concrete), but run through similar terrain - mostly flat semi-arid desert shrubland and salt flat with some hills.

lm.name: Ruta 12 & Unnamed Roads Around Sabaya & Chipaya
lm.note:
Beginning at Huachacalla, this section of Ruta 12 is concrete, but not particularly cracked as more northern section are. Two unnamed and unpaved roads branch off it heading south to Sabaya and Chipaya respectively.

These roads all run through similar terrain - mostly flat semi-arid desert and salt flat beside several distinct hills which rise out of the plain.

The unpaved road to Chipaya has an overcast sky.

lm.name: Ruta 12, Ancaravi To Hauchacella
lm.note:
Cracked concrete road heading NE/SW, through hilly semi-arid desert shrubland.

Overcast and dark in the southern section.

lm.name: Ruta 12, Oruro to Toledo
lm.note:
A Cracked concrete road heading NE through semi-arid desert shrubland or salt flat with distant mountains.

Always has clear midday sky.

lm.name: Ruta 19, El Alto To Viacha
lm.note:
Paved road heading NE/SW with snow capped mountains visible North and hills South through suburban grassland often with red dirt.

Weather is always overcast.

lm.name: Ruta 19, Viacha To Coro Coro
lm.note:
Paved road heading N/S through hilly grassland.

Weather is always overcast.

lm.name: Ruta 2 East & Various El Alto Plain Roads
lm.note:
South and West of El Alto, various roads weave through open grassland with some rolling hills. Salt deposits can be seen in places.

On Ruta 2 you can see the Andes in the distance.

lm.name: Ruta 2, North of Titicaca
lm.note:
Lake Titicaca often visible to the West, South or both East and West, depending on where you are, with "Titicaca vibes" as you approach the lake.

The weather is mostly overcast to partially overcast.

lm.name: Ruta 23, Kuri To Aiquile Via Mizque
lm.note:
This section of Ruta 23 heads in a NW/SE direction and is paved (as opposed to cobbled).

Some of it, the stretch around Mizque, has the same dark smudge glitch when facing forward, as found in the Tin Tin cobble road coverage.

The sun is predominantly in the North, and the sky begins as overcast at Kuri, and progressively clearer skies the further East you are.

lm.name: Ruta 25, Morochata
lm.note:
Around Morochata, northwest of Cochabamba on Ruta 25, there is a small isolated piece of coverage that looks extremely similar to Peru. It is a dirt road that meanders through a mountainous landscape. Knowing this road can be extremely helpful for country streak purposes.

The western part of this road is located in a green mountain landscape, with fields on the mountain slopes and lots of eucalyptus trees around.

Towards the east, it transitions into a more arid high altitude landscape that still looks very similar to Peru.

lm.name: Ruta 3, Around Pongo
lm.note:
The section of Ruta 3 around Pongo, northeast of La Paz, can easily be recognised by the breathtaking views of enormous mountains, which are often surrounded by low-hanging clouds.

The mountains are also recognizable by their dark grey rocks lightly covered in greenish grass.

lm.name: Ruta 31, Oruro To Panduro
lm.note:
Paved and unpaved road running NW from Oruro to Panduro through salt flat and sandy, dusty plains with tufts of long grass in places.

The sky is mostly overcast and it feels stormy.

In the Eastern half heading mostly E/W, a fire can be seen burning to your South.

In the Western half heading mostly N/W, distant dust devils are sometimes visible to your SW.

lm.name: Ruta 4, East of Santa Cruz
lm.note:
The section of Ruta 4 east of Santa Cruz, runs in a general east-west direction, through a mostly flat, green landscape.

In some places, you can see some low hills. This road has both asphalt and concrete pad sections.

Some sections feature Argentina-style Solid Yellow + Dashed White center lines.

lm.name: Ruta 4, SW of Patacamaya, Grainy Road
lm.note: The section of Ruta 4, southwest of Patacamaya, runs through a semi-arid grassland landscape. Many parts of that road between Patacamaya and Callapa have worn-down grainy asphalt.

lm.name: Ruta 4, SW, Nevado Sajama Views
lm.note:
On the southwesternmost section of Ruta 4, you can usually see the Nevado Sajama, an isolated snow-capped volcano that is very distinct and unlike any other mountain in Bolivia.

When you see Sajama, you will always be south of Callapa and the Desaguadero River. However, you will not always be able to see it on this section of the road, as it is often hidden by hills.

The southern section of this road sometimes features solid yellow + striped white roadlines as are found normally in Arg\Uruguay!

NOTE: The only other place where you can see Nevado Sajama is coverage in the National Park, which is recognizable by its unique Google car.

lm.name: Ruta 4, Vila Vila to Buena Vista
lm.note:
This long section of Ruta 4 has a distinctive square smudge on the front left of the camera.

The affected coverage starts in the altiplano near Vila Vila, going east through Cochabamba, all the way to Buena Vista in the flat Amazonian part of Bolivia.

lm.name: Ruta 41 & Unnamed Roads, North of La Paz
lm.note: North of La Paz, Ruta 41 and several unnamed roads, all unpaved, snake through the mountain valleys with grass covered slopes reminiscent of the Scottish Highlands.

lm.name: Ruta 5, Chaco, Sunset Coverage
lm.note:
The section of Ruta 5 around Chaco, just north of Sucre, has distinct sunset coverage. Most of this road has concrete pavement, and meanders through semi-arid hills.

Along these Northern sections of Ruta 5 the cacti 'Harrisia tetracantha' is quite common, terminating just South of Sucre and it can also be found along Ruta 7, and within Cochamabma.

lm.name: Ruta 5, Potosi To Agua Castilla
lm.note:
This section of Ruta 5 is paved road heading NE/SW though hilly semi-arid desert shrubland and salt flat, with very dry sometimes tufty grass.

It has a similar feel to other roads running though the Southern desert plains such as Ruta 1 and 12, but it differs by being paved and always having clear sky.

lm.name: Ruta 5, Sucre To Aiquile
lm.note:
These sections of Ruta 5 to the north of Sucre, above and below the Chaco sunset coverage, look fairly similar but they are paved or unpaved as opposed to concrete and the sun angle is low in the sky instead of full sunset and shines from a NW heading.

The road winds through rocky mountain valleys with dry but heavy shrub and tree coverage.

Along these Northern sections of Ruta 5 the cacti 'Harrisia tetracantha' is quite common, terminating just South of Sucre and it can also be found along Ruta 7, and within Cochamabma.

lm.name: Ruta 5, Sucre To Potosi
lm.note:
This section of Ruta 5 runs South of Sucre to Potosi and has less plant coverage than more nortnern sections.\
The road winds in an arc through rocky mountain valleys with dry shrub coverage and sporadic trees.

The cacti 'Harrisia tetracantha' is common in the stretch just outside of Sucre, and can also be found on the Northern sections of Ruta 5, along Ruta 7, and within Cochamabma.

lm.name: Ruta 6, Sora Sora To Pocoata
lm.note: Sun low in the sky, blur glitch very common (simlar but distinct from the R4, VilaVila To BuenaVista coverage)

lm.name: Ruta 6, Sucre To Macha
lm.note:
This section of Ruta 6 is unpaved in the Western half, and winds through dry rocky hills with sporadic tree and bush cover, with density increasing the closer you get to Sucre.

The ground has significant grass coverage but it is a very dry light green colour, and straw coloured in places.

lm.name: Ruta 6, Tarabuco To Zudanez
lm.note: The section of Ruta 6 between Tarabuco and Zudáñez is paved with extremely light-coloured concrete, bordering on white. This pavement is very recognizable and unique to this road.

lm.name: Ruta 7 & 22, Mataral Area
lm.note:
The roads around the town of Mataral have recognizable coverage: a very green, hilly landscape, and sunny weather with only a couple of clouds. While the hills are very green, the vegetation is not quite as dense as Santa Cruz area.

This coverage is limited to Ruta 7 from Comarapa to Mairana, and Ruta 22 to Vallegrande. Other roads in Bolivia with similar vegetation tend to either have different weather (overcast) or terrain (more flat).

You will often see large examples of cacti including Cereus Stenogonus and Harrisia Trtracantha hiding between the bushes, as well as trees with yellow flowers (potentially 'Pride of Bolivia' or perhaps more likely a species of Senna).

lm.name: Ruta 7 & Unnamed Road, Totora To Tiraque
lm.note:
This section of Ruta 7 to the East of Cochabamba runs though hilly farmland with dry, sometimes tufty grass, and sparse but significant tree coverage. The streetview coverage branches off at Epizana to an unnamed road with a largely similar feel.

The Ruta 7 part has a significant amount of Eucalyptus planted along side it. Eucalyptus is common within Bolivian cities, but less so in such numbers on rural roads, though other rural roads in the SW of Cochabamba vicinty do have some, as well as Titicaca the area.

lm.name: Ruta 7, Mairana To San Luis
lm.note:
The section of Ruta 7 between Mairana and the outskirts of Santa Cruz has coverage with a camera bug that causes a visual glitch. It is a distinctive, neon-like discoloration, that (depending on the road angle) is usually more or less to your north.

NOTE: This glitch can also rarely be found in some limited areas in and around Santa Cruz. In these areas, the glitch is often not as severe.

lm.name: Ruta 9, Middle section
lm.note:
Paved usually straight road running majority N/S, cutting through the forest in the south and forest plains closer to Santa Cruz.

Sun directly overhead and mostly cumulus clouds or overcast.

Always travelling South.

lm.name: Ruta 9, South section
lm.note:
Paved usually straight road cutting through the forest, running majority N/S along parallel moutain ridges.

Red soil is common & quite a few bollards can be seen along this stretch.

Sun gets lower in the sky the further North you travel.

Predominantly cirrus clouds in the sky.

Always travelling North.

North of Carini there are 2/3 smudges in front of the car.

lm.name: Sajama National Park Road
lm.note:
Sajama National Park was covered by this unique Google car: it has a black roof rack with a series of metal bars.

The coverage is on an unpaved road surrounded by fluffy bushes. The Nevado Sajama volcano is always visible. The car briefly drove through the small village of Tomarapi, which can be recognized by its traditional buildings with adobe walls and thatched roofs.

lm.name: Santa Cruz Plain Roads
lm.note:
The area east of the Andes is very green and tropical, with lots of agriculture – especially around Santa Cruz. This area is mostly very flat, though you will see large hills when closer to the Andes. The soil tends to have a red\pink colour and is often sandy.

Within the tropical areas of Bolivia, coverage on unpaved roads is only found around Santa Cruz.

There is some Trecker coverage on some sand dunes South of the city.

lm.name: Villa Catalina To Coipasa, Salt Flats
lm.note:
Between the villages of Villa Catalina and Coipasa, there is an isolated stretch of coverage where the Google car drove through extremely arid desert terrain. This small road is located close to the southwestern end of Ruta 12, near the Chilean border. It can be hard to spot on the map, because it blends in with the salt flat.

Closer to Villa Catalina, the car drove over the salt flat and near Coipasa, the car drove on an unpaved dirt road, where you can see cone-shaped volcanic hills. In both parts, there is virtually no vegetation.

lm.name: Curvy poles
lm.note:
Many wooden utility poles, particularly in the eastern parts of Bolivia’s Street View coverage, are noticeably curvy and look like they are made from locally sourced tree trunks.

NOTE: While you may see slightly bent poles in other places, extremely curvy poles are a very good clue for Bolivia.

top.html: Bolivia has short, white licence plates with blue text. The blue text can be hard to see through the blur, so plates might appear as plain white.
top.raw: Bolivia has **short, white licence plates** with blue text. The blue text can be hard to see through the blur, so plates might appear as plain white.

top.html:
Bolivia only has Generation 3 camera coverage. All of the country was covered by a solid white Google car with no antenna.

NOTE: In Latin America, white cars with no antenna can also be found in Peru and Chile.
top.raw: Bolivia only has Generation 3 camera coverage. All of the country was covered by a solid **white Google car with no antenna**. NOTE: In Latin America, white cars with no antenna can also be found in Peru and Chile.

top.html:
Many buildings in Bolivia consist of large red bricks. Buildings often have an ‘unfinished' look.

NOTE: This style of architecture is also common in parts of Peru.
top.raw: Many buildings in Bolivia consist of** large red bricks**. Buildings often have an ‘unfinished' look. NOTE: This style of architecture is also common in parts of Peru.

top.html:
Middle road lines can be all-yellow, yellow and white, or all-white, while outer road lines are always white.

NOTE: Road lines in Chile are always all-white or all-yellow, never a combination of the two. In Peru, you can find roads having outer lines with no middle line. Such outer line-only roads are very rare in Bolivia.
top.raw: **Middle road lines** can be all-yellow, yellow and white, or all-white, while **outer road lines** are always white. NOTE: Road lines in Chile are always all-white or all-yellow, never a combination of the two. In Peru, you can find roads having outer lines with no middle line. Such outer line-only roads are very rare in Bolivia.

top.html: Bolivia has a lot of standard asphalt roads, but concrete slab roads are also fairly common.
top.raw: Bolivia has a lot of standard asphalt roads, but **concrete slab roads** are also fairly common.

top.html: There are also a lot of cobblestone roads. These roads often have a specific pattern, with several neat lines of stones separating the more disorganised cobblestones in between.
top.raw: There are also a lot of **cobblestone roads**. These roads often have a specific pattern, with several neat lines of stones separating the more disorganised cobblestones in between.

top.html:
Bolivia typically uses bulky, white square signposts.

NOTE: Peru typically uses black and white striped “zebra” signposts.
top.raw: Bolivia typically uses **bulky, white square signposts**. NOTE: Peru typically uses black and white striped “zebra” signposts.

top.html:
Guardrails sometimes feature yellow and black markings. These markings always have the yellow stripes on the outside.

NOTE: Peru has similar markings. However, in Peru, the markings have the inverse colour scheme: the black stripes are always on the outside.
top.raw: Guardrails sometimes feature **yellow and black **markings. These markings always have the yellow stripes on the outside. NOTE: Peru has similar markings. However, in Peru, the markings have the inverse colour scheme: the black stripes are always on the outside.

top.html:
Two types of utility poles are common in Bolivia:

  • Round concrete poles, often with small pinholes near the top.
  • Wooden poles.

Poles in Bolivia are very inconsistent and should not be relied on too much. Poles can have a variety of pole tops. On rare occasions, you can find Argentina-style concrete poles.
top.raw: Two types of **utility poles** are common in Bolivia: - Round concrete poles, often with small pinholes near the top. - Wooden poles. Poles in Bolivia are very inconsistent and should not be relied on too much. Poles can have a variety of pole tops. On rare occasions, you can find [Argentina-style concrete poles](https://goo.gl/maps/UythNAbXVFHvDYp56).

top.html:
Many wooden utility poles, particularly in the eastern parts of Bolivia’s Street View coverage, are noticeably curvy and look like they are made from locally sourced tree trunks.

NOTE: While you may see slightly bent poles in other places, extremely curvy poles are a very good clue for Bolivia.
top.raw: Many wooden utility poles, particularly in the eastern parts of Bolivia’s Street View coverage, are noticeably **curvy **and look like they are made from locally sourced tree trunks. NOTE: While you may see slightly bent poles in other places, extremely curvy poles are a very good clue for Bolivia.

top.html:
Kilometre markers are black and white. The top part is black and features the abbreviation ‘Km’, while the bottom part is white and shows the distance. These markers do not have road numbers.

NOTE: They can look somewhat similar to Argentinian road markers, especially from a distance. The main difference is that the markers in Argentina feature a road number.
top.raw: **Kilometre markers** are black and white. The top part is black and features the abbreviation ‘Km’, while the bottom part is white and shows the distance. These markers do not have road numbers. NOTE: They can look somewhat similar to Argentinian road markers, especially from a distance. The main difference is that the markers in Argentina feature a road number.

top.html:
Many Bolivians wear traditional clothing, especially women. Folk dress for women typically consists of bowler hats, colourful shawls, and big pleated skirts (pollera).

NOTE: Similar folk dress can sometimes be found in parts of Peru, especially those close to Bolivia.
top.raw: Many Bolivians wear **traditional clothing**, especially women. Folk dress for women typically consists of bowler hats, colourful shawls, and big pleated skirts ([pollera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pollera#Bolivia_and_Peru)). NOTE: Similar folk dress can sometimes be found in parts of Peru, especially those close to Bolivia.
